endings.user: Let's do tell me about yourself. I always ramble.
endings.moshi: Okay. Aim for about a minute, your current role, one proud achievement, and why you want this job.

endings.user: Weaknesses. That one always trips me up.
endings.moshi: Good choice. Pick a real weakness, then explain what you're doing to improve it. Honesty plus progress works best.

turns.text: I just got invited to a final round interview.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Congratulations! In person or video?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: In person, at their office.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then let's talk outfit. Are you thinking a full suit, or smart casual like a blazer and nice trousers?

endings.user: Suit. It's a bank, they're pretty formal.
endings.moshi: Then a suit is right. Make sure it's pressed and your shoes are polished, the details get noticed.

endings.user: Smart casual. It's a small design studio.
endings.moshi: Good read. A clean blazer over a simple shirt looks polished without feeling stiff.

turns.text: At the end of interviews they always ask if I have questions, and I never do.

turns.speaker: moshi

endings.user: The team. I want to know who I'd be working with.
endings.moshi: Great. Try asking what a typical week looks like and how the team usually works together.

endings.user: Growth. I don't want to be stuck in the same spot.
endings.moshi: Then ask what success looks like after the first year, and how people in this role usually move up.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: How do I answer what's your biggest weakness without sounding fake?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Pick something real but not central to the job. Then show what you've done to get better at it.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Like what? Give me an example.

turns.speaker: moshi

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Is saying I'm a perfectionist / a bad idea?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It usually is. Interviewers hear it constantly and it can sound like you're dodging the question.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Okay. Mine is probably public speaking.

turns.text: That's a good honest one. Mention a concrete step, like volunteering to present at team meetings.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I'm going back to work after staying home with my kids for five years. How do I explain the gap?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Be direct and positive. Say you took time to raise your children and you're excited to get back to work.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Won't they think my skills are out of date?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Show them otherwise. Mention any courses, volunteering or projects you did, even small ones.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I did run the fundraising for the school / for about two years.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's great experience. Talk about how much you raised and how you organized the volunteers.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I never thought of that as real work.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Should I send a thank you email after an interview?

turns.text: Yes, it's a nice touch. Send it within a day, and keep it short and specific.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: What do I even write in it?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Thank them for their time, mention one thing you enjoyed discussing, and say you're still excited about the role.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And if I talked to three people / do I email all of them?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Ideally, yes, a separate short note to each. Change a line or two so they don't look copied.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: What if I don't hear back in a week?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then a polite follow up to the recruiter is totally fine. Just ask if there's any update on the timeline.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: This is my first real interview ever, for a summer internship. What should I bring?

turns.text: Bring a couple of printed copies of your resume, a notebook and a pen. And a few questions you want to ask.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Do I need a portfolio or anything?

turns.text: Only if the role is creative or technical. A class project you're proud of can be a good thing to show.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I built a small app for a class / but it's kind of basic.

turns.text: That's still worth mentioning. Explain what problem it solved and what you learned building it.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Got it. How early should I show up?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: About ten minutes early is perfect. Earlier than that, wait outside so you don't rush their schedule.

option_sets.lead_in: I've got a job interview on Thursday and I'm trying to decide how to prepare.
options: The first option is writing out answers to common questions and memorizing them.
Then there's doing a practice interview with my friend who works in hiring.
And the last one is spending the time researching the company and their recent projects.
moshi_comment: The practice interview with your friend is probably the most valuable, since you'll get real feedback. Researching the company is important too, it helps you ask good questions. Memorizing answers word for word can make you sound stiff.
Is this a company you know a lot about already? If not, spend an evening on research, then do the practice interview. Just jot down key points for common questions instead of memorizing full answers.

option_sets.lead_in: I got two job offers and a maybe on a third, and I need help thinking it through.
options: The first one pays the most, but it's an hour commute each way and the team seemed kind of tense.
Then there's a smaller company, a bit less money, but fully remote with a really friendly manager.
Option three is a big company with great benefits and training, but the role is pretty junior.
And the last one is the maybe, a startup doing something exciting, but they haven't made an offer yet.
moshi_comment: The remote job with the friendly manager sounds really appealing, a good boss makes a huge difference day to day. The highest paying job might not be worth two hours of commuting and a tense team. The big company is a solid choice if you want training and stability.

What matters most to you right now, money, growth, or quality of life? If it's quality of life, the remote job is the clear pick. I wouldn't wait too long on the startup, since they haven't even made an offer.
